client: I've been really struggling ever since I got my diagnosis a few weeks ago. Every single day I wake up with this knot in my stomach, just dreading what might happen next or how things might get worse. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the diagnosis is real and no amount of reframing is going to make it go away.
therapist: What you're carrying sounds really heavy, and I want you to know that your skepticism about therapy makes complete sense — you're right that we can't change the diagnosis itself, and I'd never want to minimize how real and frightening this is. What CBT can help with isn't erasing the hard truth, but exploring whether some of the thoughts that greet you each morning — like the dread of *what might happen next* — are adding an extra layer of suffering on top of what's already real. I'm curious, when that knot in your stomach shows up first thing, what kinds of specific thoughts or images tend to come with it?

client: When I wake up, the first thing that usually hits me is this image of myself completely incapacitated, like unable to work or take care of myself, and people around me either pitying me or just... drifting away because I've become too much of a burden. Then there's this thought that just loops: "this is only going to get worse, and there's nothing you can do about it." I guess I can see what you mean about an extra layer, but it's hard to separate what's realistic fear from what's just my mind spiraling, because some of those worst-case scenarios could actually happen.
therapist: That image of isolation and becoming a burden, paired with that looping thought — that sounds exhausting to wake up to every single day, and I really hear how hard it is to untangle "possible" from "inevitable." You've actually named something really important: some worst-case scenarios *could* happen, but our minds often treat "could happen" as "will happen" and skip straight to living there, which adds real suffering now to pain that may or may not come. I'm wondering — when you imagine those people drifting away, is that based on anything you're actually seeing in how they're responding to you right now, or is it more of a fear your mind is projecting forward?

client: Honestly, it's probably more projection than anything I'm actually seeing right now — most people have been kind and checking in on me since the diagnosis. But here's the thing, I keep wondering if that's just the "early days" kindness, like people showing up because it's new and they feel obligated, and eventually that will fade when my situation becomes more long-term or demanding. So even when I try to tell myself it's just fear, there's this part of me that feels like I'm just setting myself up to be blindsided if I let my guard down.
therapist: It's really meaningful that you can already see the projection happening — that's genuinely hard to do, and it tells me you have more insight into your own mind than you might give yourself credit for. What I'm noticing is that your mind has found a clever way to stay protected: even when the evidence is kind, it reframes that kindness as temporary, so the fear never really has to be challenged. I'm curious — has there been a relationship in your life, maybe before this diagnosis, where someone *did* stay through something long and difficult, and what was that like?

client: There is one person — my friend Dara — who stuck around through a really rough patch I had about five years ago when I lost my job and kind of fell apart for a while. She showed up consistently, even when I wasn't great company, and that did last, not just the first few weeks. But I find myself thinking that a chronic health condition is different, that it's a longer and heavier ask, and I'm not sure it's fair to expect anyone to sign up for that indefinitely.
therapist: Dara sounds like someone who showed you something really important — that you *have* been worth staying for, even when things were hard and messy. I gently want to reflect back what I'm hearing though: you're essentially telling yourself that you don't deserve ongoing support, that asking for it long-term is somehow unfair or too much — and I wonder if that belief might be doing more to push people away than your health condition ever would. What do you think Dara herself would say if you asked her whether she sees caring for you as an unfair burden?

client: Honestly, I know Dara would probably push back hard on the idea that I'm a burden — she's told me before that she wants to be there for me, and I do believe she means it in the moment. But there's still this voice that says believing her fully is naive, like I'm just setting myself up for disappointment if I lean into that and then one day it shifts. I think what you're pointing out about the belief pushing people away is uncomfortable to hear, because part of me suspects you might be right, but I don't really know how to stop protecting myself from that fear.
therapist: There's something really courageous in what you just said — sitting with that uncomfortable possibility that the self-protection itself might be part of the problem takes real honesty. What I want to gently offer is that we're not aiming to get you to *stop* protecting yourself entirely, but to notice that right now your mind is treating Dara's love as a threat to be defended against, rather than something real to lean into — and that's a painful and lonely way to live. I'm wondering, what would it feel like, even just as a small experiment, to let yourself believe her a little more fully — not forever, not naively, but just enough to see what happens?

client: The idea of it feels almost like stepping off a ledge, which I know sounds dramatic, but that's genuinely how it registers in my body — like if I let myself fully believe I'm worth that kind of sustained care, I'm making myself vulnerable in a way I can't take back. I think part of what makes this hard is that the diagnosis already took away so much of my sense of control, and keeping some emotional distance feels like one of the few things I can still manage. So I'm not saying no to the experiment, but I guess I'm asking — what does "believing her a little more" even look like in practice, because right now it feels abstract and I'm not sure where to start.
therapist: It doesn't sound dramatic at all — it sounds like someone who has already lost a lot of certainty trying to protect the little that remains, and that makes complete sense. In practice, "believing her a little more" might start somewhere very small and concrete, like the next time Dara checks in, instead of deflecting or minimizing how you're doing, you answer her one degree more honestly than feels comfortable — not everything, just one small truth. I'm wondering, is there something real about how you're feeling right now that you've been holding back from Dara, something small enough to feel manageable but true enough to feel like a real step?

client: There is something, actually — I've been telling Dara that I'm "doing okay, just taking it one day at a time" every time she asks, but the truth is that some mornings I'm really not okay and I feel terrified and alone in a way I haven't told anyone. I think I could maybe tell her that, just that one thing, that some mornings are genuinely scary. But I'm already feeling anxious about it, because what if saying it out loud makes it more real, or what if she doesn't quite know what to do with it and there's this awkward moment that changes things between us?
therapist: What you just identified is really significant — you've been carrying those terrifying mornings completely alone, and the fact that you can name exactly what you want to share with Dara tells me you're closer to ready than the fear is letting you believe. The worry that saying it out loud makes it more real is so understandable, but I'd gently offer that those mornings are already real — you're living them alone right now, and telling Dara doesn't create the fear, it just means you'd no longer have to hold it by yourself. And if there is an awkward moment where she doesn't quite know what to say — what do you think that would actually mean about her, or about you?

client: I guess an awkward moment wouldn't actually mean she doesn't care — it might just mean she's human and doesn't have the perfect response ready, and that's not really a reflection of my worth. That reframe makes some logical sense to me, but I notice I'm still bracing for it emotionally, like my body hasn't caught up with what my head is processing. I think I'm willing to try telling her, but I'm worried I'll lose my nerve in the moment or default back to "I'm fine" without even realizing I'm doing it.
therapist: That gap between what your head understands and what your body feels is completely normal — insight often arrives before the emotional system catches up, and that's not a failure, it's just how change actually works. One thing that can help with losing your nerve in the moment is to plan something small and concrete beforehand, like even sending Dara a text rather than waiting for the "right" in-person moment, which removes some of the pressure of a live reaction. Would it feel more manageable to start there — maybe even thinking about what you'd want that message to say?

client: A text does feel less terrifying than saying it face to face, so that part actually helps. I'm thinking something like "hey, I just wanted to be honest that some mornings since the diagnosis have been really scary and I haven't been telling you that" — but even typing that out in my head right now makes my chest tight, because once I send something like that there's no taking it back. I think I'll try it, but I'm not going to promise myself a timeline because I don't want to turn it into another thing I feel guilty about if I don't follow through.
therapist: That message you drafted is honest, clear, and genuinely brave — and the chest tightness you feel around it is actually a sign that it matters, not a sign that it's wrong. I really respect that you're not forcing a timeline on yourself; that's not avoidance, that's self-compassion, and there's an important difference between the two. When you do feel ready, that message is already there waiting for you — and I'm curious, how are you feeling right now, in this moment, compared to when we first started talking today?

client: Honestly, I feel a little lighter than when I came in, which surprises me because I didn't expect to get anywhere today given that the diagnosis itself hasn't changed. I think what shifted is that I came in feeling like I had to carry all of this completely alone, and now I'm at least considering that I don't have to. But I want to be honest that I'm also a little scared that this feeling won't last, that I'll wake up tomorrow with that same knot in my stomach and all of this will feel far away again.
therapist: That shift you're describing — from "I have to carry this alone" to "maybe I don't" — is actually a meaningful change, even if it feels fragile right now. And you're probably right that tomorrow morning might still bring that knot, because one conversation doesn't rewire patterns that have been protecting you for a long time — but here's what will be different: you'll have had this moment, and you can't unknow what you recognized today. I'm wondering, if that knot does show up tomorrow morning, what's one small thing you could remind yourself of — maybe something from today — that might make it even just slightly less heavy?
